dedupe_keys.name: space weather drivers of the egnos service degradation on 10 october 2024

description: This study analyses why the European Geostationary Navigation Overlay Service (EGNOS) suffered significant degradation of its Safety of Life service over the Mediterranean region on 10 October 2024. The authors trace the full Sun-to-Earth chain, from solar eruptions to ionospheric effects on GNSS signals, and find that the most severe signal degradation occurred during the passage of a sheath region after an interplanetary shock, with scintillation affecting more than 40% of tracked satellites at some locations. It covers the storm day over the Mediterranean, using one-minute Local Disturbance indices computed at five INTERMAGNET observatories (Memambetsu, Iznik, San Fernando, Fredericksburg and Honolulu), the S4 amplitude scintillation index from 50 Hz GNSS measurements at the ALCA station in Alcalá de Henares with satellite azimuth and elevation, and public indices, solar wind data and IGS observations. The work is by M. Flores-Soriano, C. Cid, A. Collado-Villaverde, I. Maseda-Zurdo and A. Reche; the derived data were deposited on Zenodo on 29 July 2026 under CC BY-NC 4.0, with files restricted while the paper is under review. Caveats: the files cannot yet be downloaded, and one scintillation station limits spatial detail. It supports hazard exposure and resilience analysis of satellite navigation services to space weather; a related record is the Skibotn GNSS scintillation and TEC data.
